design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (DerSimonian-Laird; meta-regression with cluster-robust variance) of double- or triple-blind randomized placebo-controlled trials (parallel or crossover) of methylphenidate products approved or under FDA consideration in children and adolescents aged 6 to 18 with ADHD, conducted in clinical or naturalistic settings and reporting sleep-related adverse events, either spontaneously reported (coded to MedDRA terms) or elicited with rating scales. 35 trials gave 75 observations; pooled relative risks by MedDRA sleep category, meta-regressions of design and sample features, an ad hoc adjustment of each product's relative risk for confounders, and a model predicting the relative risk from the placebo adverse-event rate. Funded by a manufacturer of one of the compared products.
can_establish: How much more often sleep-related adverse events (insomnia and its subtypes, 'sleep disorder') were recorded with methylphenidate than with placebo in blinded trials in young people with ADHD up to August 2017, and which trial features go with larger or smaller relative risks.
cannot_establish: How many children per 100 had sleep problems on methylphenidate or placebo (absolute rates are not reported in the text); the effect on sleep measured objectively; effects in adults or with non-prescribed use; the trustworthiness of each trial (not appraised); and fair comparisons between products, given the funder's stake and a non-standard adjustment method.

sample.recruitment: Trials found in PubMed, Ovid (PsycInfo, EMBASE, Medline) and Web of Knowledge from inception to 18 August 2017, plus ClinicalTrials.gov, FDA medical reviews and labels, and reference lists; English only.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: double- or triple-blind randomized placebo-controlled trials, parallel or crossover; children or adolescents 6 to 18 with DSM-III or later ADHD or ICD-9 or later hyperkinetic disorder; methylphenidate products approved or under FDA consideration; clinical or naturalistic setting; sleep reported as spontaneous or elicited adverse events; English. Two studies using a global sleep rating that could not be coded were excluded.
sample.demographics: Not tabulated in the main text (covariates such as mean age, percentage male and percentage of Caucasian participants were extracted for meta-regression; details in supplementary tables not read).
sample.attrition: Not reported at review level; many screened studies lacked usable data (authors' limitations).
sample.selection_effects: Industry-dominated trial literature of approved products in young people with ADHD; English only; trials enrolling stimulant responders had lower relative risks, and many trials enrolled people previously treated with stimulants, which selects against those who stopped because of side effects.

exposure.measurement: Randomized methylphenidate products against placebo under double or triple blinding.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as described by the review: immediate-release methylphenidate and several extended or delayed-release products (osmotic-release oral system, transdermal system, delayed-release and extended-release HLD200, multilayer-release beads, PRC-063, extended-release dexmethylphenidate, long-acting, CD and sustained-release forms), dosed once, twice or three times a day, with dose strategies classified by prior stabilization or optimization and forced titration; no doses are given in the text. Extended-release products had higher mean relative risks for sleep-related adverse events than immediate-release ones (4.8 against 1.9, p = 0.03), and once-daily products higher than twice-daily or three-times-daily ones (4.6 against 1.7 and 2.5); the authors attribute this to doses taken too late in the morning or to differences in how long products act, and treat these features as properties of the products, not confounders.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (clinical trials of a prescribed medicine); exclusion for psychiatric comorbidity was extracted as a covariate.

comparison.controls: Placebo arms of the same blinded trials (2606 patients).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Sleep problems are common in untreated ADHD; the placebo arm's adverse-event rate stands in for baseline propensity, which the review shows strongly predicts the relative risk.

outcomes.instruments: Spontaneously reported adverse events coded to MedDRA or COSTART terms (insomnia, initial, middle and terminal insomnia, combined insomnia, early morning awakening recoded as terminal insomnia, sleep disorder), or elicited by rating scales or questionnaires using clinical cut-points coded to the same categories plus sleep duration.
outcomes.validity_norms: Adverse-event recording depends on how it was elicited; the authors show that design features and the placebo rate shape the relative risk.
outcomes.operationalization: A sleep-related adverse event as a recorded MedDRA-coded complaint or a rating above a clinical cut-point; no objective sleep measure.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (six sleep categories pooled, plus many meta-regressions).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The trials were double- or triple-blind by inclusion; the review did not assess blinding integrity or other risk-of-bias domains.

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled relative risks, methylphenidate against placebo: insomnia RR 1.61 (z = 9.2, p < 0.001); initial insomnia 2.78 (z = 6.6, p < 0.001); middle insomnia 2.97 (z printed as 183, p < 0.001); combined insomnia 2.97 (z = 6.4, p < 0.001); sleep disorder 1.99 (z = 4.2, p < 0.001). No confidence intervals, heterogeneity statistics or absolute rates are given in the text. Editors' calculation of 95% CIs from RR and z (assuming z = ln RR / SE): insomnia 1.45 to 1.78; initial insomnia 2.05 to 3.77; combined insomnia 2.13 to 4.15; sleep disorder 1.44 to 2.74; middle insomnia not computable. Drug and placebo adverse-event rates correlated r = 0.89 (p < 0.0001); the placebo rate was associated with the relative risk (z = -3.3, p = 0.001) and with the product studied (chi2 = 21.0, p = 0.01).
analysis.covariates: Meta-regressions of mean age, percentage male, percentage stimulant responders, year, number of sites, dosing strategy, rater and rating-scale use, and placebo adverse-event rate; missing covariate values entered as a separate category.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned (page searched).
analysis.selective_reporting: Terminal insomnia appears in the Discussion as significantly associated with methylphenidate but has no pooled result in the Results; per-trial values are only in figures.
analysis.power: Not addressed; 35 trials and about 5700 patients give precise pooled relative risks, but per-product comparisons rest on few trials.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In blinded trials in young people with ADHD, recorded insomnia was about 1.6 times as frequent with methylphenidate as with placebo, and initial and combined insomnia about 2.8 to 3 times as frequent, with 'sleep disorder' about twice as frequent. Most individual trials' adjusted relative risks did not differ from 1, some were below 1, and the size of the relative risk depended strongly on how often the placebo group reported sleep problems and on design features.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and discussion say several types of insomnia, including terminal insomnia in the Discussion, are associated with methylphenidate and that products differ after adjustment. Gaps: (1) terminal insomnia has no reported pooled estimate; (2) no interval or absolute rate accompanies any pooled estimate, although the authors themselves warn that relative risks cannot be read without absolute risks; (3) the product comparison uses an unvalidated adjustment and was funded by the maker of a competing product, with its employees extracting data; (4) the trials were not appraised. The authors' central methodological point, that the placebo rate constrains the relative risk, is shown clearly.

timeline.event: Kidwell et al., meta-analysis of stimulant medicines and objectively and subjectively measured sleep in young people with ADHD (Pediatrics), in the library's reference list but not read for this card.
This meta-analysis of sleep-related adverse events in methylphenidate trials, the first on this question by the authors' account.

replication.where_it_stands: The sleep-related adverse-event signal for methylphenidate in young people with ADHD is consistent at the pooled level; its size in absolute terms, its objective counterpart and any product differences remain to be read from other sources (for example kidwell_2015).

funding.funder: Manuscript development funded by Ironshore Pharmaceuticals & Development, Inc. (subsidiary of Highland Therapeutics Inc.); two Ironshore employees (PharmDs) assisted with data extraction. Faraone is also supported by the K.G. Jebsen Centre (University of Bergen), EU FP7 grant 602805, EU Horizon 2020 grants 667302 and 728018, and NIMH grants 5R01MH101519 and U01 MH109536-01.
funding.declared_conflicts: Faraone received income, potential income, travel expenses, continuing education support and/or research support from Otsuka, Lundbeck, KenPharm, Rhodes, Arbor, Ironshore, Shire, Akili Interactive Labs, Alcobra, Enzymotec, Sunovion, Genomind and NeuroLifeSciences, and holds a US patent (US20130217707 A1) on sodium-hydrogen exchange inhibitors for ADHD. Cortese received travel and accommodation reimbursement from ACAMH. Komolova and Po are employees of Highland Therapeutics Inc.
funding.affiliations_note: Ironshore's product, delayed-release and extended-release methylphenidate (HLD200), is among the products compared; two of the four authors and two data extractors were employees of the funder or its parent.

what_would_settle_it: An independent, registered meta-analysis using individual-participant or arm-level data that reports absolute rates of sleep problems with methylphenidate and placebo by age, product and how problems were elicited, appraises each trial, and adds objective sleep measures; and comparable data in adults, including non-prescribed use.

domains.note: Sources of variation in the relative risk were investigated by meta-regression and discussed at length, including the role of the placebo rate.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: items 8 and 10 can be judged only from a supplement that was not read; they are non-critical and cannot change the rating. Five critical items are 'no' (2: no protocol; 7: no excluded-study list; 9: no appraisal of the trials; 11: pooled estimates without intervals or heterogeneity and non-independent observations; 13: risk of bias not considered, which follows from 9), while 4 is partly met and 15 met, which under AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. The review may be cited for the direction and approximate size of the pooled relative risks of recorded sleep complaints in blinded trials in young people with ADHD (with the editors' intervals labelled as such) and for its demonstration that the placebo rate constrains the relative risk; not for comparisons between products, given the funder's stake.

key_findings.finding: 35 blinded randomized placebo-controlled trials in children and adolescents with ADHD, with 75 observations of sleep-related adverse events, were included: 3079 patients on methylphenidate and 2606 on placebo (search to 18 August 2017).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Study Selection; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Pooled relative risks, methylphenidate against placebo: insomnia 1.61 (z = 9.2), initial insomnia 2.78 (z = 6.6), middle insomnia 2.97 (z printed as 183), combined insomnia 2.97 (z = 6.4) and sleep disorder 1.99 (z = 4.2), all p < 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' 95% CIs from RR and z: insomnia 1.45 to 1.78; initial insomnia 2.05 to 3.77; combined insomnia 2.13 to 4.15; sleep disorder 1.44 to 2.74. No absolute rates are reported in the text.

key_findings.finding: For the insomnia category, the adjusted relative risks of individual trials varied widely: more than 75% did not differ significantly from 1, some were significantly below 1 and some above 1. Egger's test showed no evidence of publication bias (t = 0.37, p = 0.7).
key_findings.locator: Results › Meta-Analysis of Odds Ratios Adjusted for Confounders, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 legend

key_findings.finding: Mean age, percentage male, percentage of stimulant responders, year of publication, number of sites, dosing strategy, type of rater and use of rating scales were associated with both the relative risk and the product studied; very young samples had higher and nearly all-male samples lower relative risks; clinician raters without rating scales produced higher relative risks.
key_findings.locator: Results › Assessment of Potentially Confounding Variables, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The type of product was associated with the relative risk: longer-acting products had higher relative risks than immediate-release ones (values in the exposure field); after the authors' adjustment, products differed for initial insomnia, insomnia and sleep disorder, with the highest relative risks for the osmotic-release, transdermal and PRC-063 products.
key_findings.locator: Results › Assessment of Potentially Confounding Variables, 3rd paragraph; Results › Meta-Analysis of Odds Ratios Adjusted for Confounders, 3rd paragraph; Figure 4 legend

key_findings.finding: Drug and placebo adverse-event rates were highly correlated (r = 0.89, p < 0.0001), and the observed relative risks were close to those predicted from the placebo rate alone; because the drug-group rate cannot exceed 100%, a placebo rate of 50% caps the relative risk at 2.0.
key_findings.locator: Results › The Impact of Placebo AE Rates on the RR Statistic; Figure 5 legend

key_findings.finding: The authors note that eliciting adverse events with questionnaires yields higher absolute rates in both arms but smaller relative risks than spontaneous reporting, so relative risks should not be compared across trials without considering absolute risks.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th and 9th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The pooled relative risk for middle insomnia is printed as 2.97 with z = 183, an implausible test statistic, and the same relative risk (2.97) is printed for combined insomnia (z = 6.4).
reporting_issues.consequence: The middle-insomnia estimate cannot be used; its interval cannot be reconstructed.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says methylphenidate was significantly associated with terminal insomnia, but the Results report no pooled estimate for terminal insomnia and the abstract does not list it.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Terminal insomnia should not be cited as an established effect from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: No confidence interval, heterogeneity statistic or absolute rate is given for any pooled estimate in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Absolute risks (how many children per 100) cannot be stated; intervals are editors' calculations from z.

reporting_issues.issue: Identical Egger test results (t = 0.37, p = 0.7) are reported for two different sets of trials (Figures 2 and 3).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Meta-Analysis of Odds Ratios Adjusted for Confounders, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two results is probably a copying error; the publication-bias assessment for the insomnia subtypes is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The section heading speaks of odds ratios although every analysis uses relative risks, and the paragraph on Figure 3 refers to relative risks in Figure 4.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Meta-Analysis of Odds Ratios Adjusted for Confounders, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Editorial errors; the measure is the relative risk throughout.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the DerSimonian-Laird model computes a pooled relative risk weighted by sample size; that model weights by inverse variance.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The weighting actually used is uncertain.

verification.first_pass_by: AI (Claude, reading agent), AI reader 111 (first reader)
verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC8074661 (author manuscript; all sections, acknowledgements and disclosures read; Figures 1 to 5 and the prediction equation are images and their values were not extracted; the supplementary .docx file was not opened)

design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of studies that randomly assigned children and adolescents with ADHD to stimulant conditions and measured sleep by actigraphy or polysomnography: 9 studies, 246 young people; methylphenidate in 6 (Corkum, Galland, Gruber, Sangal, Schwartz, Tirosh) and amphetamine-class medicines in 3 (Chatoor; Giblin & Strobel, lisdexamfetamine; Santisteban, mixed amphetamine salts). Hedges' g compared baseline nights (or, in 4 studies, placebo nights) with medicated nights for sleep latency, sleep efficiency and total sleep time; trim-and-fill for publication bias; study-level moderator regressions. CINAHL, PsycINFO and PubMed searched from February 2014 to March 2015.
can_establish: The average direction and standardized size of differences in objectively measured sleep onset, efficiency and duration between medicated and unmedicated nights in small published studies of young people with ADHD.
cannot_establish: Differences in minutes (only standardized effects are given), the randomized effect against placebo (most comparisons use pre-treatment nights), effects in adults or with non-prescribed use, adaptation within children over time (the duration moderator compares 7 studies), or the trials' risk of bias (coded but not reported).

sample.recruitment: 9927 records screened, 167 full texts examined, 158 excluded (list in the supplement, not read), 9 included (p. 5).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Children or adolescents diagnosed with ADHD, random assignment to stimulant conditions, sleep measured by actigraphy or polysomnography; excluded if key statistics were unavailable after contacting authors; no restriction on country or year (p. 2).
sample.demographics: Mean ages 102 to 139 months (about 8.5 to 11.6 years); 41.7% to 85.3% boys; 7 to 50 participants per study (Table 1, p. 4).
sample.selection_effects: Published studies only. One included study is titled a matched case-control study (Galland et al., 2010) despite the randomization criterion. Schwartz et al. (2004) and Gruber et al. (2006) come from the same group and share a mean age of 110.4 months, so their samples may overlap (editors' observation; not addressed by the review).

exposure.measurement: Assigned stimulant condition in each study (Table 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions (Table 1): 2 to 49 days on medication; mean total daily dose 15.6 to 48.75 mg where reported; 1 to 3 doses a day; short-, medium- and long-acting forms; oral. One condition per study was used (mixed amphetamine salts in Santisteban et al.; the low-dose condition in Corkum et al.) (pp. 2-3).

comparison.controls: Each child's own unmedicated baseline sleep, or placebo nights in the 4 studies that did not report baseline (p. 3).

outcomes.instruments: Actigraphy in most studies; polysomnography in Chatoor et al. and Galland et al. (and in Giblin & Strobel for latency, by Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Polysomnography described as the gold standard; it showed larger efficiency effects than actigraphy (p. 7).
outcomes.operationalization: Sleep latency, sleep efficiency and total sleep time; other sleep variables too sparsely reported (p. 3).

analysis.effect_sizes: Hedges' g, random effects: sleep latency 0.78 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.02), Q(6) = 18.35, I2 67.30%; trim-and-fill (3 studies imputed) 0.54 (0.28 to 0.81). Sleep efficiency -0.39 (-0.69 to -0.08), I2 83.37%; trim-and-fill (1 imputed) -0.32 (-0.63 to -0.01). Total sleep time -0.59 (-0.84 to -0.35), I2 82.67%, no asymmetry. Moderators (study level): latency effect larger with more doses a day (b = 0.42 per extra dose, k = 5, p = .001); efficiency effect smaller with more days on medication (b = 0.05 per day, k = 7) and more nights recorded (0.04 per night), larger with polysomnography (-0.81) and with a higher share of boys (-0.02 per percentage point); no moderators for total sleep time. Single studies: latency 0.44 to 1.15; efficiency -1.76 to 0.48; total sleep -1.31 to -0.16 (Table 1).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable (moderator regressions one at a time).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration mentioned; PRISMA followed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only three of the coded sleep variables were analysed because others were too sparsely reported.
analysis.power: Seven studies per outcome; moderator analyses with 4 to 7 studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 9 small studies, medicated nights showed longer sleep onset (g 0.78; 0.54 after trim-and-fill), lower sleep efficiency (-0.39) and shorter sleep (-0.59) than unmedicated, mostly pre-treatment, nights, with high heterogeneity.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say that stimulant medications “impair the sleep of children and adolescents” (p. 9), and the review stresses that it included only randomized trials. Gaps: (1) the effect sizes mostly compare medicated nights with pre-treatment nights, not the randomized placebo contrast, so the strength of randomization does not carry over to the estimates; (2) the trials' risk of bias was coded but neither reported nor used; (3) the dose-frequency and duration moderators come from 5 to 7 studies but are offered as guidance for prescribing; (4) no difference in minutes is given.

timeline.event: Cortese et al., meta-analysis of subjective and objective sleep in children with ADHD (cited as background, ref. 7).
This meta-analysis of objectively measured sleep on stimulants.
Faraone et al., meta-analysis of sleep-related adverse events in placebo-controlled methylphenidate trials; a different outcome (reported events) from a partly overlapping literature.

replication.where_it_stands: The objective-sleep counterpart of the adverse-event meta-analyses; both point the same way, but the literatures overlap, so they are not fully independent. A meta-analysis of the placebo contrasts with sleep in minutes is still missing.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no financial relationships or conflicts of interest (p. 9).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Nebraska-Lincoln. Four of the nine included studies were coded as funded by a pharmaceutical company (Table 1; Gruber et al. is coded both ways).

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant-data meta-analysis of placebo-controlled randomized trials with actigraphy or polysomnography, reporting minutes of sleep onset and total sleep by formulation and by weeks since starting, with repeated measurement over months.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 can only be judged from the supplement, which was not read. Critical items 2, 9, 11 and 13 are not met (4 partly; 15 met), so confidence is critically low whatever item 7 shows. The direction of the pooled effects is consistent, but the numbers are mostly before-after contrasts within children, converted with assumptions, from trials whose risk of bias is not reported.

key_findings.finding: From 9927 records and 167 full texts, 9 studies (246 young people) were included; inclusion required random assignment to stimulant conditions and actigraphy or polysomnography.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Methods › Study Selection (p. 2); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Effect sizes compared baseline with medicated sleep; where a study gave no baseline, its placebo nights were used (4 studies); when the correlation between conditions was unknown, a between-subject effect was computed with r assumed to be 0.5.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data Extraction; Effect Size Calculation

key_findings.finding: Sleep latency: 7 samples (N = 171), g = 0.78 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.02), I2 67.30%; after trim-and-fill (3 studies imputed) 0.54 (0.28 to 0.81).
key_findings.locator: Results › The Effect of Stimulant Medications on Sleep Latency, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Sleep efficiency: 7 samples (N = 155), g = -0.39 (-0.69 to -0.08), I2 83.37%; after trim-and-fill (1 study imputed) -0.32 (-0.63 to -0.01). The negative effect was smaller in studies with more days on medication (b = 0.05 per day) and more nights recorded, and larger with polysomnography and with more boys.
key_findings.locator: Results › The Effect of Stimulant Medications on Sleep Efficiency (p. 6); Table 3 (p. 7)
key_findings.note: Negative values checked on the rendered pages; the text layer drops the minus sign.

key_findings.finding: Total sleep time: 7 samples (N = 223), g = -0.59 (-0.84 to -0.35), I2 82.67%; no funnel-plot asymmetry; no significant moderators.
key_findings.locator: Results › The Effect of Stimulant Medications on Total Sleep Time (pp. 6-7); Table 4 (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Latency effect larger in studies with more doses a day (b = 0.42 per additional dose, k = 5, Q(1) = 10.24, p = .001); no other moderator of latency was significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Sleep Latency, 2nd paragraph; Table 2 (p. 6)
key_findings.note: A study-level comparison of 5 studies about the dosing schedule; kept out of claims (no regimen in claims).

key_findings.finding: Single-study effects (Table 1): latency 0.44 to 1.15 (all longer on medication); efficiency -1.76 to 0.48 (one study, Giblin & Strobel, better on medication); total sleep -1.31 to -0.16 (all shorter).
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (read on the rendered, rotated page)

key_findings.finding: No external funding; the authors declare no conflicts of interest.
key_findings.locator: Financial disclosure; Funding; Potential conflict of interest

reporting_issues.issue: Heterogeneity for sleep latency is printed as Q(6) = 18.35, P = .054; Q = 18.35 on 6 degrees of freedom gives p = 0.0054 (editors' calculation), consistent with the printed I2 of 67.30%.
reporting_issues.consequence: A decimal error; heterogeneity for latency is significant, not borderline.

reporting_issues.issue: After trim-and-fill imputed 3 (latency) and 1 (efficiency) studies, the Q statistics are still given with 6 degrees of freedom.
reporting_issues.consequence: The adjusted heterogeneity tests are misreported or mislabelled.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives Q(1) = 0.62, P = .043 for method of latency assessment; Q = 0.62 on 1 degree of freedom gives p = 0.43 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The moderator is not significant, as the text says; the printed p is a decimal error.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives N = 155 for sleep efficiency, while the Table 1 efficiency rows sum to 159 (editors' sum).
reporting_issues.consequence: The participant count for this outcome is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 codes Giblin & Strobel as polysomnography with N = 12 in the latency rows but actigraphy with N = 16 in the efficiency rows, codes Gruber et al. as pharmaceutically funded in the efficiency rows but not in the total-sleep rows, and prints the total-sleep rows without a heading, so they appear to continue the efficiency block.

design_detail: Two-phase clinical study in a hospital ADHD programme in Vancouver: 10 nights of baseline, then sleep-hygiene instruction for all children (an uncontrolled before-after phase), then, for those whose insomnia persisted, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of melatonin (two 10-day periods, each followed by 5 days of placebo washout), then 90 days of open-label melatonin for responders (Figure 1, p. 515). Sleep from parent sleep diaries (somnologs) and wrist actigraphy. The card's design and risk-of-bias rating refer to the randomized phase.
can_establish: Within the randomized phase, whether melatonin shortened the time to fall asleep compared with placebo in children with ADHD on stimulant medicine whose initial insomnia persisted after a sleep-hygiene run-in.
cannot_establish: The effect of sleep hygiene itself (no control group), the effect of melatonin without prior sleep hygiene, in children not taking stimulants or with other sleep disorders (excluded; no polysomnography), long-term effects under blinding (the 90-day phase was open-label and limited to responders), or daytime effects beyond a clinician's global rating and a parent ADHD scale.

sample.recruitment: Clinical referrals to the Provincial ADHD Program, British Columbia Children's Hospital (pp. 514-515).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 6 to 14; ADHD (DISC-IV, Child Symptom Inventories, confirmed by a clinician); stimulant dose unchanged for at least 2 months; mean sleep-onset latency over 60 minutes on 10 nights of parent diaries; parents able to keep diaries; child able to wear an actigraph and accept a fixed bedtime. Excluded: stressful circumstances, bed-sharing or other environmental causes, medical or psychiatric illness linked to insomnia or needing other sedating or activating medicines, several households unless all caregivers could take part, known major sleep disorders (not screened by polysomnography) (p. 514).
sample.demographics: 90.9% boys; mean age 10.29 (6.5 to 14.7); 87.9% white; 67% on methylphenidate (a third OROS) and 30% on dextroamphetamine; 54% with oppositional disorder, 12% enuresis; sleep problem rated mild in 3.0%, moderate 42.4%, marked 30.3% and severe 24.2% (p. 516).
sample.attrition: Five of 33 withdrew before randomization; of 23 eligible, 1 withdrew and 3 were discontinued for protocol violations, leaving 19 analysed per protocol; the authors say results did not differ materially when the others were included (p. 515).
sample.selection_effects: Motivated families able to follow the programme; children who responded to sleep hygiene were removed before randomization, so the trial sample was enriched for persisting insomnia.

exposure.measurement: Pharmacy-dispensed blister cards; at least 80% adherence required in each phase (p. 515).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: short-acting pharmaceutical-grade melatonin 5 mg made by the sponsor, taken 20 minutes before bedtime, for 10 days per period (p. 515). Sleep hygiene: a consistent bedtime and waking time with a target of at least 9.5 hours in bed within age norms, no caffeine and no naps, reviewed with parents from 10 nights of diaries (p. 514).
exposure.polysubstance: All children took stimulants at stable doses; other medicines and natural products were monitored (p. 515).

comparison.controls: Placebo in the crossover, each child serving as his or her own control; for the sleep-hygiene phase, the child's own baseline.
comparison.matching: Within-person; order randomized in blocks of four by the pharmacy (p. 514).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Undiagnosed primary sleep disorders were possible, since no polysomnography was done (p. 517).

outcomes.instruments: Parent-completed somnolog (parents checked every 15 minutes whether the child was asleep); wrist actigraph with proprietary software; Clinical Global Impression-Improvement; Conners ADHD scale, parent version (CADS-P); adverse events (p. 515).
outcomes.validity_norms: Actigraphy reliability cited; diary and actigraph sleep-onset latencies correlated r = 0.76 after sleep hygiene (p. 516).
outcomes.operationalization: Primary: mean sleep-onset latency (time from being put to bed to falling asleep) in each phase, from the diaries; secondary: night-to-night variability, total sleep, actigraph measures, responders (much or very much improved), ADHD symptoms.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Children, parents and staff were blind to treatment order in the randomized phase; the sleep-hygiene and open-label phases were unblinded.

analysis.effect_sizes: Sleep hygiene (before-after, no control): diary latency 91.7 to 69.3 minutes (t(28) = 2.77, p = .01) and actigraph 98.1 to 73.0 (t(21) = 2.92, p < .01); effect size 0.67; diary variability 47.7 to 29.1 minutes (t(28) = 3.81, p < .01); 5 responders (latency under 60 minutes); 21% rated much or very much improved. Melatonin against placebo: diary latency 46.4 (SD 26.4) against 62.1 (SD 26.6) minutes, t(20) = -3.06, p < .01, with a significant period effect, t(20) = -2.20, p < .05, and no carryover; effect size 0.6; actigraph latency t(18) = -4.54, p < .01; diary total sleep 15.0 minutes longer, t(20) = 3.13, p < .01; actigraph total sleep and variability not different; clinician ratings and CADS-P not different. Open label (responders only): latency 31 minutes, sleep duration 23 minutes longer (t(12) = 3.90, p < .01). Baseline to end of open label: 91 to 31 minutes, effect size 1.7. Adverse events: 20% of all events during melatonin and 23% during placebo; one severe migraine; rash from the actigraph band in two (pp. 516-517).
analysis.covariates: Period adjusted for in the crossover analysis (Senn).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or published protocol is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Actigraph latency means for the randomized phase are not given; the text attaches the 16-minute difference to the actigraph, while the diary means differ by 15.7 minutes.
analysis.power: Planned to detect a 30-minute change with 25 children (80% power, 20% dropout allowed); 19 were analysed and the observed difference was about 16 minutes (p. 515).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Melatonin shortened parent-recorded time to fall asleep by about 16 minutes against placebo (effect size 0.6) in about 20 children, with a concordant actigraph result, no difference in clinicians' global ratings or ADHD symptoms, and mild adverse events as frequent as on placebo; sleep hygiene was followed by an uncontrolled improvement of about 22 to 25 minutes.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that combined sleep hygiene and melatonin was “a safe and effective treatment for initial insomnia” (p. 512), citing a combined effect size of 1.7 and a 60-minute fall. Gaps: (1) the 1.7 and the 60 minutes are uncontrolled before-after figures at the end of open-label treatment in the 17 children chosen as melatonin responders; (2) safety rests on 10 days of blinded melatonin in about 20 children; (3) the sleep-hygiene effect has no control group; (4) clinicians' ratings of improvement did not differ between melatonin and placebo.

timeline.event: Weiss et al., pilot crossover trial in 9 children with ADHD (as described, p. 514).
Tjon Pian Gi et al., open-label study of melatonin in 24 children with ADHD (as described, p. 514).

replication.where_it_stands: One small sponsor-funded crossover trial; other trials of melatonin in children with ADHD (not read here) should be read before any stronger statement.

funding.funder: Investigator-initiated trial sponsored by Circa Dia BV, which made the melatonin (pp. 512, 515).
funding.declared_conflicts: First author: consultant, advisory board or speaker's bureau member, or holder of research contracts or grants with Eli Lilly, Shire, Janssen Ortho, Novartis, Purdue, Johnson & Johnson and Circa Dia; the other authors none (p. 518).
funding.affiliations_note: University of British Columbia; Provincial ADHD Program; British Columbia Children's Hospital.

what_would_settle_it: A registered, adequately powered parallel-group trial of melatonin against placebo in children with ADHD and stimulant-related insomnia, with and without sleep hygiene in a factorial design, analysed by intention to treat, with diaries, actigraphy and daytime outcomes and blinded follow-up over months.

domains.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
domains.note: Order randomized by the pharmacy in blocks of four; baseline comparison between sequences planned (results not shown).

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects
domains.note: Five-day placebo washout and no significant carryover, but a significant period effect (sleep latency changed over time regardless of treatment); the analysis adjusts for period.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Double-blind; but three children were discontinued for protocol violations and the analysis is per protocol.

domains.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
domains.note: Four of 23 eligible children are missing from the stated analysis (17%); the degrees of freedom suggest more children were analysed than the 19 stated (reporting issue 1).

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Blinded parent diaries and objective actigraphy agree in direction.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registration; several secondary outcomes; actigraph means not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 for the randomized crossover. Allocation and blinding were sound and the main outcome was measured blind; the concerns are the per-protocol analysis with unexplained numbers, the period effect, and the absence of registration. The rating does not cover the sleep-hygiene and open-label phases, which are uncontrolled.

key_findings.finding: Thirty-three children consented; 5 withdrew, 5 responded to sleep hygiene, 23 were eligible for randomization, 1 withdrew and 3 were discontinued for protocol violations, leaving 19 analysed per protocol; 17 continued into open-label follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Results › Patients, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Sleep hygiene (no control group): mean latency fell from 91.7 to 69.3 minutes on diaries (t(28) = 2.77, p = .01) and from 98.1 to 73.0 on actigraphy (t(21) = 2.92, p < .01), effect size 0.67; only 5 children fell below an hour; clinicians rated 21% much or very much improved, 21% minimally improved, 54% unchanged and 4% minimally worse; ADHD ratings did not change.
key_findings.locator: Results › Response to Sleep Hygiene, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Melatonin against placebo: diary latency 46.4 (SD 26.4) against 62.1 (SD 26.6) minutes, t(20) = -3.06, p < .01, effect size 0.6; significant period effect t(20) = -2.20, p < .05; no carryover; actigraph latency also shorter, t(18) = -4.54, p < .01.
key_findings.locator: Results › Melatonin Versus Placebo, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Negative t values checked on the rendered page (the text layer prints the minus sign as 'j').

key_findings.finding: Diary total sleep was 15.0 minutes longer on melatonin (t(20) = 3.13, p < .01); actigraph total sleep and night-to-night variability did not differ; clinicians' improvement ratings and ADHD ratings did not differ between melatonin and placebo.
key_findings.locator: Results › Melatonin Versus Placebo, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Adverse events were mild or moderate except one severe migraine; the only study-related event was a rash from the actigraph band in two children; 20% of all adverse events were reported during melatonin and 23% during placebo.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety

key_findings.finding: Open label in the 17 melatonin responders: latency 31 minutes at the end, not different from the randomized melatonin phase; sleep duration 23 minutes longer (t(12) = 3.90, p < .01); baseline to end, 91 to 31 minutes, effect size 1.7.
key_findings.locator: Results › Open-Label Follow-up; Outcome of Combined Treatment

key_findings.finding: The trial was sponsored by the maker of the melatonin, and the first author reported financial ties with several makers of ADHD medicines and with the sponsor.
key_findings.locator: Title page footnote (p. 512); Disclosure (p. 518)

reporting_issues.issue: The randomized-phase tests have 20 (diary) and 18 (actigraph) degrees of freedom, which for this crossover analysis implies about 22 and 20 children, while the text says results are for the 19 who completed per protocol.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which children were analysed is unclear; the per-protocol N may not be the analysis N.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 27 children received sleep hygiene; the participant flow gives 28 (33 consented minus 5 withdrawals), and the paired test has 28 degrees of freedom (29 children).
reporting_issues.consequence: The sleep-hygiene sample size is uncertain by one or two children.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give full remission with sleep hygiene or both treatments in 71% (p. 517), the Discussion 81% responding to sleep hygiene, melatonin or both (p. 518).
reporting_issues.consequence: The proportion who benefited cannot be quoted reliably.

reporting_issues.issue: The open-label sleep-duration test has 12 degrees of freedom (13 children), though 17 entered open-label follow-up.
reporting_issues.consequence: Missing data in the open-label phase are not explained.

reporting_issues.issue: Medicine use adds to 97% (67% methylphenidate, 30% dextroamphetamine).
reporting_issues.consequence: One child's stimulant is not stated; minor.
